key_insight: Plane-major rows make precision a fetch knob: fetching 4 of 16 planes activates ~1/4 of the rows. Most useful for KV-score screening and batch-1 decode.
killer_doubt: An ACT senses the whole 8 KB row, so column selection saves only I/O. Storing FP16 planes to read 4 uses 4x the DRAM of a static INT4 copy.
decisive_experiment: Software trace study (~$30k): Llama-70B decode at batch 1, 32 and 128 in a plane-major layout. Count rows activated and bytes moved at equal perplexity against a static INT4/FP8 copy.
prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024); SpAtten (HPCA 2021) fetches MSBs first; Matryoshka Quantization (2025); BitWeaving bit-sliced scans (SIGMOD 2013).

key_insight: Exact interval bounds let an MSB-first plane fetch stop with no accuracy loss wherever a top-k or argmax consumes the result: LM-head sampling, MoE routing, vector retrieval.
killer_doubt: With 4 of 16 planes, worst-case slack (sum|x|*max|w|/16) is ~40 logits, above ~10-20 logit gaps. Linear layers have no exact stop; the LM head is ~1.5% of 70B weights.
decisive_experiment: GPU emulation (<$30k): interval-bound early termination on a Llama-70B LM head, KV key scoring and a FAISS-scale kNN index at batch 1-64. Report the fraction of planes skipped and the share of total decode bytes saved.
prior_art: BitWeaving/V bit-sliced scans with early pruning (SIGMOD 2013); SpAtten progressive quantization; Energon multi-round mixed-precision filtering; SnaPEA early termination (ISCA 2018).

key_insight: One plane-major copy serves several precisions, so precision is chosen per access instead of per stored copy. A software or FPGA demo is cheap.
killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-08176. Shipping models already store INT4/FP8 (0.5-1 B/param). A 16-plane master copy costs 2 B/param, the wrong direction while DRAM costs 4x.
decisive_experiment: Fold into I-08176's trace study. No separate experiment is warranted.
prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024) serves 3-8-bit models from one bit-plane copy; Stripes and Bit-Fusion bit-serial accelerators.

key_insight: An FPGA controller that remaps plane-major weights over a link is a cheap, concrete prototype of fetching precision on demand.
killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-08176 and I-01714. Reading 4 planes of stored FP16 moves the same link bits as a native 4-bit model but holds 4x its capacity.
decisive_experiment: Fold into I-08176's trace study. No separate experiment is warranted.
prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024); bit-plane weight layouts in bit-serial accelerators (Stripes, Bit-Fusion).

key_insight: Tail IDs carry little learned information, so a generator plus an explicit cache of the hottest 1% could shrink multi-TB tables 10-100x without new wafers.
killer_doubt: A DHE-class decoder (k=1024, ~1800-wide MLP) costs ~1e7 MACs (~5 uJ) per ID, against ~15 nJ to fetch 128 B. Hundreds of IDs per sample multiply dense compute ~100x.
decisive_experiment: Train DLRM on Criteo-1TB (<$40k) four ways: full table, INT4 plus pruning, CAFE hot/hash, and DHE plus a hot-1% cache. Report NE, resident GB and J/query. Drop if NE loss exceeds 0.1%.
prior_art: Deep Hash Embedding (Kang et al., KDD 2021); TT-Rec (MLSys 2021); CAFE hot-row hybrid (SIGMOD 2024); QR embeddings (KDD 2020).

key_insight: With every line driven and columns held at virtual ground, +/-V patterns make an odd-I-V crossbar exactly linear. Sneak paths become decodable, and decoding by tile suits bulk weight streaming.
killer_doubt: IR drop: a 1k-cell 20 nm Cu line (~3 kOhm) sags ~0.75 V at 1 uA/cell on a 0.2 V read; cells need >=10 MOhm. ReRAM endures 1e6-1e10, needs 3e8-7e13.
decisive_experiment: Fabricate 64x64 and 256x256 passive crossbars (ReRAM, plus fixed resistive-via ROM) at a university fab. Drive them with Hadamard patterns from a 256-channel DAC/TIA board. Measure raw BER against size, cell R and spread (~$400k).
prior_art: Zidan et al., multiport closed-form sneak-path readout (IEEE TNANO 2014, via search snippet); Strukov passive 4K crossbars; Cassuto sneak-path coding. Compressed-sensing readout: none found.

key_insight: Putting compression in the CXL controller, off the CPU critical path, and compressing only far-tier lines fixes the latency failure of MXT. Capacity grows with no new wafers.
killer_doubt: Already commercial. Fleet data show ~20-30% of memory cold at ~3x compression, a ~15-25% gain, not 33-60%. Where host encryption (SEV/TDX) covers the memory, lines are ciphertext and compress ~1.0x.
decisive_experiment: Nothing beyond a replay (~$20k): run public far-memory traces, plus sampled SEV/TDX-encrypted VM pages, through base-delta and LZ4 models to bound the fleet capacity gain.
prior_art: ZeroPoint Technologies CXL compression IP; Marvell Structera A inline LZ4; OCP hyperscale CXL tiered-memory compression; IBM MXT (2000).

key_insight: Diffusion-style local balancing needs no global allocator. A gradient-and-lease protocol is cheap to simulate and could simplify the control plane of multi-switch CXL fabrics.
killer_doubt: Microsoft Pond measured ~7% DRAM saving at 16-socket pools, not 10-15%. Each CXL switch hop adds ~70-100 ns, and multi-hop lease recalls when the gradient flips risk thrashing.
decisive_experiment: Replay Azure and Google cluster traces (~$30k) through a pooling simulator, comparing gradient diffusion with a central allocator at 8-64 sockets. Report stranded DRAM recovered, migration bytes and recall stalls.
prior_art: Microsoft Pond (ASPLOS 2023); Meta TPP (ASPLOS 2023); Cybenko diffusion load balancing (1989); CXL 3.x fabric-manager pooling.

key_insight: Retired DDR4 is a real supply buffer: zero wafer starts at ~10-20% of new-bit cost. DRAM has no wear-out, so most retired dies remain good.
killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-06321. Hyperscalers already reuse DDR4 behind CXL. The CXL tier adds ~70-100 ns, and 5-7-year-old DDR4 shows HCfirst ~10k and VRT drift.
decisive_experiment: Fold into I-06321's 1,000-DIMM screening and supply census.
prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024) reuses DDR4 behind CXL; Marvell Structera and Astera Leo support DDR4 reuse.

key_insight: Harvesting at chip level, with weak-row maps in the CXL controller, can rescue packages from DIMMs that failed on only a few rows.
killer_doubt: Whole DIMMs plug into CXL cards as they are. Desoldering, baking and reballing add 1-2 reflows, rework loss and a few dollars per package, and buy only weak-row rescue.
decisive_experiment: Fold into I-06321, adding a 500-package desolder, reball and retest run to price rework yield and $/GB.
prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU; DRAM reballing and refurbishment brokers; JEDEC DDR4 post-package repair (PPR) for row remapping.

key_insight: A refurbishment line grades retired DDR4 into retention and hammer bins, then hosts each bin behind CXL with its own refresh and ECC remap, turning scrap into far memory.
killer_doubt: Supply ceiling: the server DDR4 shipped in 2019-2021 and now retiring is perhaps 6-10% of 2026 bit demand that a third party could capture. Hyperscalers keep theirs (GreenSKU).
decisive_experiment: Buy 1,000 retired DDR4 RDIMMs (~$50k). Profile 85 C retention, HCfirst and failures, and host the best bins behind a commercial CXL card. Census the decommissioned GB/yr outside hyperscalers.
prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Marvell Structera DDR4 reuse; existing resellers of refurbished DIMMs.

key_insight: A 28 nm CXL controller plus retired DDR4 needs only trailing-node capacity and no new fab, giving a cold tier for KV and page cache.
killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-06321 and I-00348. KV cache needs bandwidth: one x8 CXL card at ~32 GB/s delivers ~1/100 of an H100's 3.35 TB/s, so only the coldest KV fits.
decisive_experiment: Fold into I-06321's screening and census.
prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Marvell Structera and Astera Leo CXL controllers with DDR4 support.
